1016.title: mantra sadhana (a 40-day japa discipline)
1016.hook: a yoga Upanishad hears a mantra in the breath itself, one nobody has to say
1016.howItsDone: Some Hindu yoga teachers teach ajapa japa, listening to the breath's own sound as hamsa or so'ham and letting a chosen mantra move with the in-breath and out-breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mantra sadhana hung on the hinges of the day, dawn and dusk: stand at dawn until the sun shows, sit at dusk until the stars appear. Did you catch the light changing? Day one thousand sixteen.

Ha, on the way out. Sa, on the way in. Try listening for it the next time a room goes quiet. Breathe out through the nose, slowly, and the air makes a soft sound, close to an h. Breathe in, and there's a faint hiss, close to an s. It's easy to miss. It's just breath. But some yoga texts heard something more. To them, that soft sound was a mantra, repeated all day and all night by every breathing creature, without anyone choosing to say it. Today, the mantra that keeps itself, and what it does to the whole idea of a japa discipline.
screen: `HA, ON THE WAY OUT.` → `SA, ON THE WAY IN.` → `A MANTRA NOBODY SAYS.`

segments.voice: The text is the Dhyanabindu Upanishad, one of the yoga Upanishads. In paraphrase: the breath goes out with the sound ha and comes back in with the sound sa, and so the living being is always repeating hamsa, hamsa. This, it says, is called the ajapa gayatri. Ajapa means not-japa, or japa that isn't done. It's the repetition that happens without effort, with no beads, no lips, no count. Hamsa is also the Sanskrit word for a swan or a wild goose, a bird some texts use as a picture of the soul. Some teachers turn the sound around: so'ham, which can be heard as I am that. Either way, the idea is the same. In this teaching, a mantra is already going on in every breathing body, and the practice is to notice it. This is where the last two blocks meet. Pranayama sequences worked with the breath. Mantra sadhana works with the sound. In this teaching they turn out to be one thing. And it changes how a long sadhana can feel. For four days the practice has been about keeping something going: setting terms, counting beads, tying it to dawn and dusk. Ajapa says something quieter. The repetition isn't only the one you push. It's also the one you finally hear. Some teachers who use this keep the beads and the chosen mantra, and let the mantra ride on the breath, one sound on the out-breath, one on the in, until it's hard to tell which one is carrying which. The sadhana keeps its discipline: the terms, the beads, the hinge of the day. It just rides on a sound the breath was already making.
screen: `HA OUT, SA IN: HAMSA.` · `AJAPA: THE JAPA NOT DONE.` · `THE BREATH AND THE MANTRA MEET.` · `THE REPETITION YOU HEAR.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath move through the nose, no counting. For a few breaths, simply listen: a soft ha on the out-breath, a faint sa on the in. Don't make the sound louder. Just notice it. Then, if you've been keeping a mantra, let it rest on that sound, part on the out-breath, part on the in. If you haven't, stay with hamsa, or with the breath's own sound. When the mind drifts, come back to listening. The bell holds the time.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, ajapa: the mantra the breath keeps by itself, ha out and sa in, waiting to be heard.
Your line: one mantra, day after day. Today, once in a quiet moment, listen for three breaths to the sound the breath already makes, and let your mantra ride on it. Day one thousand sixteen.

1017.title: mantra sadhana (a 40-day japa discipline)
1017.hook: three people keep the same mantra in one house at dawn: one aloud, one in a whisper, one with no sound at all
1017.howItsDone: Hindus who keep japa may say the mantra aloud, in a whisper or silently in the mind, often counting on a mala of beads; some move between these voices within one sitting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mantra sadhana and ajapa: the mantra the breath keeps by itself, ha on the way out, sa on the way in. In a quiet moment, did you hear it, one mantra, day after day? Day one thousand seventeen.

Dawn, one house, three people, the same mantra. In the kitchen a grandmother says it out loud while the kettle heats, each syllable clear enough to hear from the hallway. On the back step her grandson whispers it, lips moving, the sound barely past his teeth. Upstairs his mother sits on the edge of the bed with her eyes closed, and nothing moves at all. No lips, no breath out of rhythm. If you walked through that house, you'd only know two of them were doing japa. All three are. An old law book sets those three voices in an order, and the order runs against the ear.
screen: `ONE HOUSE. ONE MANTRA.` → `ALOUD. WHISPERED. SILENT.` → `ALL THREE ARE JAPA.`

segments.voice: Japa is repetition: a mantra said again and again, often counted on a string of beads. In the Bhagavad Gita, chapter ten, Krishna names the best of many things to show where the divine shines through, and among sacrifices, he says, he is the sacrifice of japa. Of all the ways of offering, he names the one made of a word, said again and again. The law book called the Manusmriti goes further, and it ranks the ways of doing it. In its second chapter it says japa is stronger than the prescribed rites. Then it says japa spoken so that others can't hear it is stronger still. And japa done in the mind alone is the strongest of the three. Manu calls the quiet form upamshu, sound kept close to the lips, and the silent one manasa, of the mind. Teachers call the spoken form vachika. So the quietest voice in the house, the one nobody could hear, is the one the text sets highest. Why would that be? The text doesn't stop to explain. Some teachers read it this way: when the mantra is loud, the ear holds it for you. When it's whispered, the lips still help. When it's silent, the mind has nothing to lean on but the mind. That's harder, and that's the point. This matters for a long sadhana, a discipline kept over many days. Some teachers suggest moving between the voices rather than forcing silence. When attention scatters, go back to a whisper. When it settles, let the sound drop away. Nobody has to choose one voice forever. Read that way, the grandmother in the kitchen may be doing exactly what her mind needs at that hour.
screen: `AMONG SACRIFICES, I AM JAPA.` · `THE TEXT RANKS THREE VOICES.` · `SPOKEN, WHISPERED, MENTAL.` · `MOVE BETWEEN THEM AS THE MIND NEEDS.` · then, large: `THE QUIETEST VOICE, SET HIGHEST.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. If you've been keeping a mantra these days, use it. If not, the syllable Om will do, or a single word from your own tradition. Say it aloud a few times, gently, so you can hear it. Then let it become a whisper, lips moving, breath carrying it. Then close the lips and keep it going inside, with no sound at all. If the mind wanders, come back to the whisper for a while, then let it go silent again. The bell holds the time.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, the three voices it can be kept in: spoken, whispered and silent.

Your line: aloud, whispered, silent. Today, once in a public place, on a bus or in a waiting room, keep your mantra going with no sound and no moving lips, and notice where it goes. Day one thousand seventeen.

1018.title: mantra sadhana (a 40-day japa discipline)
1018.hook: a paper calendar on a fridge door, a row of small ticks, and one empty square in the middle
1018.carry: a long time, no break, with care
1018.howItsDone: Hindus who take on a mantra sadhana may keep it at the same time each day, sometimes as a vow made with a teacher or within the family; customs differ on what happens if a day is lost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mantra sadhana in three voices: aloud, whispered, silent. Did you try the silent one somewhere public? Where did the mantra go? Day one thousand eighteen.

A paper calendar is taped to a fridge door. Someone has been ticking off the days of a mantra practice, one small mark each morning, a neat row running across the weeks. Then, in the middle, one square is empty. A late night, a sick child, a flight. The next morning the person stands in front of that calendar holding a pen. Start the whole count over? Pretend the square isn't there? Quit, since the streak is broken anyway? Today, the last day of this stretch on mantra sadhana, we go to a short old text that has something steady to say about long practice, and nothing at all to say about streaks.
screen: `A ROW OF TICKS.` → `ONE EMPTY SQUARE.` → `START OVER, OR CARRY ON?`

segments.voice: In the first chapter of the Yoga Sutras, sutra fourteen, Patanjali says when practice becomes firmly rooted. Here it is in paraphrase: practice becomes firm when it is attended to for a long time, without a break, and with care. Three things. A long time. No break. And care, the Sanskrit word satkara, which carries a sense of honor and devotion. Notice what the sutra doesn't say. It doesn't name a number of days. Forty days is a shape teachers and families give the practice, a container. The sutra is talking about something longer than any container: a practice kept so long and so faithfully that it stops being an effort and becomes ground to stand on. A little later in the same chapter, Patanjali names a mantra. In sutras twenty-seven and twenty-eight he says the word that expresses Ishvara, the Lord, is the pranava, the syllable Om. Then he says what to do with it: its repetition, and dwelling on its meaning. Japa, and bhavana. The two go together. Saying the word and turning toward what it points to. So the empty square on the calendar matters less than the person standing in front of it. Teachers differ on whether a missed day restarts a vow, and families keep their own customs, so it's worth asking the teacher or the household whose practice it is. What the sutra holds onto is the long arc and the care. A mantra repeated with care, for a long time, until it is less something done and more something lived in.
screen: `A LONG TIME. NO BREAK. WITH CARE.` · `THE SUTRA NAMES NO NUMBER OF DAYS.` · `OM: REPEAT IT, DWELL ON ITS MEANING.` · `THE LONG ARC, NOT THE SQUARE.` · then, large: `UNTIL IT IS GROUND TO STAND ON.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath find its own pace. Take the mantra you've been keeping, or the syllable Om, or simply the breath. This time add Patanjali's second half. Repeat it slowly, and between repetitions let a moment go to what it points toward, whatever that is for you. If you pray, you can let that pointing be your prayer. If you don't, simply rest in the pause after the sound. Repeat, then pause. The bell holds the time.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline, which the Yoga Sutras say grows firm through a long time, no break, and care.

Your line: a long time, no break, with care. Today, pick one small thing you already do every day, like making tea or locking the door, and do it once with care, as if it were part of the practice. Day one thousand eighteen.

1019.title: yoga nidra
1019.hook: Vishnu sleeps on the cosmic waters, two demons rise to kill Brahma, and Brahma has to wake him
1019.carry: the goddess who holds the sleep
1019.howItsDone: Hindus who recite the Devi Mahatmya, especially during Navaratri, read Brahma's hymn to Yoganidra in its first chapter; some temples and households chant the whole text over several days.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed mantra sadhana with Patanjali: practice grows firm through a long time, no break, with care. Which small daily thing did you do with care? Day one thousand nineteen.
screen: `MANTRA SADHANA.` · `A LONG TIME. NO BREAK. WITH CARE.`

segments.voice: Everything is water. One age of the world has ended, and the next hasn't begun. On that ocean, on the coils of a great serpent, Vishnu lies asleep. From his navel rises a lotus, and on the lotus sits Brahma, the one who will make the next world. Then two demons, Madhu and Kaitabha, rise out of the dark and come for Brahma. He looks down at the one person who could help him, and Vishnu doesn't stir. This sleep isn't ordinary. It has a name, and the name is today's word.
screen: `ONE OCEAN. VISHNU ASLEEP.` → `TWO DEMONS COME FOR BRAHMA.` → `THE SLEEP HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: The story is the opening of the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, a text set inside the Markandeya Purana. Here's what Brahma does, in paraphrase. He doesn't shake Vishnu. He doesn't shout. He turns to the power that is holding Vishnu asleep, and he praises her. The text calls her Yoganidra. Yoga nidra: the sleep of yoga. And in this story she isn't a technique. She is the Goddess herself, the great power behind creation and its keeping and its ending, and Vishnu's sleep is one of her forms. Brahma's hymn calls her by many names, among them the great night and the night of delusion, and also intelligence and understanding. Then he asks her to let Vishnu go. And she does. The text says she withdraws from his eyes, his mouth, his nose, his arms, his heart and his chest, and the Lord of the world rises. He fights Madhu and Kaitabha, and in the end they're undone. So the first thing the phrase yoga nidra carries, on this path, is a picture: a sleep that isn't absence. Vishnu isn't knocked out. He rests on the waters held by a power so great that even the creator has to ask her permission to wake him. Over the coming days we'll follow this idea into the Upanishads, into Patanjali, and into the guided practice people now do lying on a mat. But it begins here, on the water, with a sleep so full it has its own name and its own hymn.
screen: `BRAHMA PRAISES THE ONE WHO HOLDS THE SLEEP.` · `YOGANIDRA IS THE GODDESS HERSELF.` · `SHE LEAVES HIS EYES, HIS HEART. HE RISES.` · `A SLEEP THAT ISN'T ABSENCE.` · then, large: `YOGA NIDRA: THE SLEEP OF YOGA.`

segments.voice: If you can, lie down, or lean back in your chair. Let the body be heavy, as if resting on water. Let the eyes close. Now follow the story's waking, slowly, in reverse. Feel the chest, rising and falling. Then the heart area. The arms, resting. The nose, the breath moving in it. The mouth, soft. The eyes, still behind the lids. Don't try to sleep and don't try to stay alert. Just rest and notice. The bell holds the time.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga. In the Devi Mahatmya, it's the Goddess herself, holding Vishnu asleep on the waters.

Your line: the goddess who holds the sleep. Tonight, as you lie down, notice the moment just before sleep, and see whether you can rest there for one breath before it takes you. Day one thousand nineteen.

1020.title: yoga nidra
1020.hook: every night we pass through three worlds, and a short Upanishad says there's a fourth
1020.carry: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth
1020.howItsDone: Hindus who study Vedanta read the Mandukya Upanishad's four states, sometimes with Gaudapada's Karika beside it; some chant Om slowly, resting in the silence after the sound.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra began on the cosmic waters: Vishnu asleep, held by the Goddess Yoganidra, the goddess who holds the sleep, and Brahma praising her to wake him. Did you catch the moment before sleep last night? Day one thousand twenty.
screen: `YOGA NIDRA.` · `THE GODDESS WHO HOLDS THE SLEEP.`

segments.voice: A night of sleep has borders in it. Somewhere around lights out, the room and the to-do list let go, and pictures start arriving on their own. A dream. Later, even the pictures stop, and there's nothing at all, no dream, no self to report it. Then morning, and the room comes back. Waking, dreaming, deep sleep. That is the road through a night. The Mandukya Upanishad maps it, and then it does something surprising. It says there's a fourth.
screen: `THE ROOM LETS GO.` → `PICTURES ARRIVE.` → `THEN NOTHING. THEN MORNING.`

segments.voice: The Mandukya Upanishad begins with a word from the mantra days just behind us: Om. All this is Om, it says, and this Self has four quarters. Here they are, in paraphrase. The first is the waking state, knowing outward, enjoying the world of things. The second is the dreaming state, knowing inward, enjoying what is subtle. The third is deep sleep, where the sleeper wants nothing and sees no dream. The text doesn't call it empty. It calls it a gathered mass of knowing, full of bliss, the doorway to knowledge. And then the fourth, turiya, which the text describes mostly by what it is not. Not knowing outward, not knowing inward, not a mass of knowing. Unseen, beyond grasp, peaceful, one without a second. That, it says, is the Self, and that is what is to be known. Then the Upanishad maps the four onto the sound of Om. The A is waking. The U is dreaming. The M is deep sleep. And the fourth has no part at all, beyond the sound; some teachers hear it as the silence after Om ends. So here's what this does for yoga nidra. The practice that goes by this name today lies down right on those borders, between waking and dreaming, between dreaming and sleep. Its teachers describe it as staying aware while the body falls asleep. The Mandukya gives that idea a map. Sleep isn't only a switch going off. It's a set of rooms, each with its own kind of knowing, and the text points past all of them to the one who was there through every room.
screen: `ALL THIS IS OM. THE SELF HAS FOUR QUARTERS.` · `WAKING, DREAMING, DEEP SLEEP.` · `THE FOURTH: NOT IN, NOT OUT. PEACEFUL.` · `A, U, M, AND THE SILENCE AFTER.` · then, large: `TURIYA: THE FOURTH.`

segments.voice: Lie down if you can, or sit back and let the eyes close. Say Om once, aloud or in the mind, slowly. Feel the A open in the throat, the U round in the mouth, the M hum at the closed lips. Then let it end, and stay in the quiet after it. When thoughts come, let them come, like pictures at the edge of sleep. When it feels right, say Om once more, and again rest in the silence that follows. The bell holds the time.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga, resting on the borders the Mandukya maps: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth beyond them.

Your line: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth. Tomorrow morning, before you open your eyes, try to notice which room you're coming out of: a dream, or nothing at all. Day one thousand twenty.

1021.title: yoga nidra
1021.hook: a king asks a sage what light a person sees by when the sun, moon and fire are all gone
1021.howItsDone: Hindus who study the Upanishads read Janaka's questions to Yajnavalkya on the light of the Self and on dream and deep sleep; teachers of yoga nidra describe the practice as resting deeply while staying aware.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra and the Mandukya's map: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth. This morning, which room were you coming out of? Day one thousand twenty-one.

A king named Janaka puts a question to the sage Yajnavalkya. What light does a person see by? The sun, says the sage. By its light we sit, go out, work, and come home. And when the sun has set? The moon. And when the moon has set? Fire. And when the fire goes out? Then speech: in the dark, we move toward a voice. And when speech, too, falls silent? The king keeps pushing, the way a child keeps asking why. The answer is where this Upanishad turns toward sleep.
screen: `WHAT LIGHT DOES A PERSON SEE BY?` → `SUN. MOON. FIRE. SPEECH.` → `AND WHEN ALL OF THEM ARE GONE?`

segments.voice: This is the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, chapter four, and Yajnavalkya's answer, in paraphrase, is this: then the Self is his light. By that light he sits, goes out, works and comes home. Then the sage follows the person into sleep. In dreams, he says, there are no chariots, no harnesses, no roads. But the dreamer makes chariots and harnesses and roads. There are no joys or ponds or rivers, and the dreamer makes those too. In dream, the text says, the person becomes his own light. Nothing outside is lighting the scene. It's lit from within. And then comes the image this whole yoga nidra stretch could rest on. A falcon, or any swift bird, has been flying around in the open sky. It grows tired. It folds its wings and is carried down to its nest. In the same way, the sage says, a person hurries toward that state where, asleep, there's no more wanting and no more dreaming. Deep sleep, here, isn't collapse. It's a homecoming. The falcon isn't shot down. It folds its own wings. Sleep is where the reaching stops. So when a teacher of yoga nidra asks a room full of people to stop doing and let the body grow heavy, they're inviting something this Upanishad already pictured: the wings folding, the bird going home. The difference the practice adds is staying aware as it happens. The falcon lands, and some part of us watches it land.
screen: `THEN THE SELF IS HIS LIGHT.` · `IN DREAMS, THE PERSON IS HIS OWN LIGHT.` · `THE TIRED FALCON FOLDS ITS WINGS.` · `SLEEP AS HOMECOMING, NOT COLLAPSE.` · then, large: `THE BIRD GOES HOME.`

segments.voice: Lie down if you can, or let the chair take your weight. Let the arms rest at your sides, palms open. Let the day so far be a long flight: all the reaching, answering, carrying. Now, on an out-breath, let the shoulders fall, as if folding wings. On the next, let the hands go slack. On the next, let the jaw soften. Each out-breath, a little more landing. Stay aware of it happening. The bell holds the time.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga. Today, the falcon folding its wings, and someone awake enough to watch it land.

Your line: the falcon folds its wings. Today, at one point when you finally sit down, let the shoulders drop on an out-breath, like wings folding, before you reach for anything else. Day one thousand twenty-one.

1022.title: yoga nidra
1022.hook: Patanjali counts sleep among the movements of the mind, not as the mind's absence
1022.carry: even sleep is a movement of the mind
1022.howItsDone: Hindus who study the Yoga Sutras read sutras 1.5–1.11 on the five vrittis, often with Vyasa's commentary, and sutra 1.38 among the ways of steadying the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra and the falcon folds its wings to go home. When you sat down, did the shoulders drop first? Today closes the week. Day one thousand twenty-two.

Here's a question that sounds like a trick. When you're in dreamless sleep, is your mind doing anything? The quick answer is no. That's the whole point of sleep: the lights are off, nobody's home. Patanjali, the teacher behind the Yoga Sutras, disagrees, quietly, in a single line. In the list where he names what the mind does, sleep is on it. Not as a break from the mind's activity. As one of its activities. That changes what it would mean to practice something called the sleep of yoga.
screen: `IS THE MIND DOING ANYTHING IN SLEEP?` → `PATANJALI PUTS SLEEP ON THE LIST.`

segments.voice: In the first chapter of the Yoga Sutras, Patanjali names the movements of the mind, the vrittis, and he gives five. Right knowing, wrong knowing, imagining, sleep, and memory. Then he defines each. Sleep, in sutra ten, in paraphrase: the movement of the mind that rests on the experience of absence. That's a careful line. Deep sleep isn't nothing. It's the mind holding onto nothing. Some commentators point to the morning as evidence: we wake and say, I slept well, I knew nothing. Something registered that nothing. So for Patanjali, sleep is still a wave on the lake, and yoga is the stilling of all the waves, sleep included. That's a reason for caution about drifting off and calling it practice. But a little later, in sutra thirty-eight, Patanjali offers sleep a different job. Among the ways he lists to steady the mind, one is this: take as support the knowledge that comes from dream and sleep. The commentators read this in more than one way. Some read it as resting the mind on the calm of deep sleep, remembered on waking. Some read it as contemplating a holy dream. Either way, the same sutras that count sleep as a movement also treat it as something to learn from. Now look back at this week. Mantra sadhana: one sound, heard riding on the breath, kept in three voices, with care, until it becomes ground to stand on. Then yoga nidra. The Goddess holding Vishnu asleep. The Mandukya's rooms of waking, dream, deep sleep, and the fourth. The falcon going home. And today, Patanjali's sober note: even sleep is something the mind does.
screen: `FIVE MOVEMENTS. SLEEP IS ONE.` · `SLEEP RESTS ON THE EXPERIENCE OF ABSENCE.` · `DREAM AND SLEEP AS A SUPPORT.` · `THIS WEEK: MANTRA, THEN SLEEP.` · then, large: `EVEN SLEEP IS SOMETHING THE MIND DOES.`

segments.voice: Lie down or sit back, and let the body grow heavy. Let a wave of drowsiness come if it wants to. Then, gently, notice it as a movement, the way you might notice a thought. Heaviness arriving. Heaviness passing. If you begin to drift, don't fight it hard. Just come back to the breath at the nose, then let the heaviness return, and watch it again. Resting and watching, both at once. The bell holds the time.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga. For Patanjali, sleep itself is a movement of the mind, and the practice is to see it as one.

Your line: even sleep is a movement of the mind. Today, the next time drowsiness comes, after a meal or on the way home, notice it arriving the way you'd notice a thought: as something the mind is doing. Day one thousand twenty-two.
